Its image is the point orbit closure, its coordinate ring is a normal domain, and the empty equation sequence is regular. The boundary is empty and has codimension $+\infty$. All conclusions follow in these cases. Henceforth $t\ge2$.

**The open chain locus.** Put $c=\sum_{i<t}n_i^2$ and $D=2\sum_{i<t}n_in_{i+1}-c$. The differential of the chain equations is $Y_iA_i+B_iX_i-X_{i-1}B_{i-1}-A_{i-1}Y_{i-1}$, with the index-zero terms zero. If each $A_i$ is injective or $B_i$ is surjective, these equations can be solved successively for any prescribed right-hand sides: use a left inverse of $A_i$ to choose $Y_i$, or a right inverse of $B_i$ to choose $X_i$, after the preceding pair is fixed. Thus the open locus $Z^\circ$ with this condition is smooth of dimension $D$ by [F4]. It is nonempty: use $U_i=\operatorname{im}e^{t-i}$, inclusions $A_i$, and restrictions $B_i=e|_{U_{i+1}}$, transported to the fixed spaces. These maps satisfy the equations and have end map $e$.

**Alternating strings and their stabilizers.** For a nilpotent pair $A:U\to W$, $B:W\to U$, the odd operator $T$ on $U\oplus W$ with these components has a homogeneous Jordan-string decomposition: kernels and images of its powers are graded, so the complements in the Jordan construction may be chosen homogeneous. Every string alternates letters $a$ from $U$ and $b$ from $W$. Removing all $b$ letters gives the Jordan rows of $BA$, and removing all $a$ letters gives those of $AB$. The ranks of alternating composites recover the numbers of strings of each length and starting letter, so a diagram determines one pair orbit and there are finitely many diagrams in fixed dimensions. The pair stabilizer is the unit group of its even endomorphism algebra, an open subset of a vector space and hence smooth and irreducible. On a string $A$ kills exactly a terminal $a$ and $B$ misses exactly an initial $a$; consequently $A$ is injective iff every string ends in $b$, and $B$ is surjective iff every string begins in $b$.

**Even orbit drops.** Distinct dominated types have strictly smaller orbit dimension. One can move from a dominating partition to a dominated one by repeatedly moving a box from an earlier row to a later allowable row: choose an excess row and a subsequent deficit row, taking the last row of the source plateau and the first allowed destination to preserve the partition inequalities, and repeat until the target is reached. A move from row $i$ to row $j>i$ increases $\sum_r(2r-1)\mu_r$ by $2(j-i)$ and therefore decreases the orbit dimension by that positive even number. Each allowable unit move from row lengths $a,b$ with $a\ge b+2$ is realized by a one-parameter degeneration. On chains $u_1,\ldots,u_{a-1}$ and $v_1,\ldots,v_{b+1}$ of the destination type, keep the usual lowering maps except send $v_{b+1}$ to $v_b+z u_{a-1}$, with $v_0=0$. At $z=0$ the type is $(a-1,b+1)$; for $z\ne0$ the ranks of powers are those of $(a,b)$ (the chain generated by $v_{b+1}$ has length $a$, and the remaining chain has length $b$). Keeping other strings fixed proves that dominated types belong to the top orbit closure. Hence a drop of exactly two consists of one box moved to the next row; any other drop is at least four. Equivalently, parity also follows from $\sum_j(\mu'_j)^2\equiv\sum_j\mu'_j=N\pmod2$ for the total sum; individual summands in a difference of square sums need not be even.

**The pair-orbit dimension.** Write $m=\dim U$, $n=\dim W$, and let $E,O$ be the dimensions of the even and odd centralizers of $T$. A homomorphism between Jordan strings of lengths $L,L'$ has $\min(L,L')$ possible shifts. Counting the parity of those shifts, odd strings of the same endpoint type contribute $+1$ to the even-minus-odd count, and odd strings of opposite type contribute $-1$; the two opposite Hom directions for an odd/even pair cancel, and even/even pairs contribute zero. Summing gives $E-O=(m-n)^2$, because the difference between the numbers of odd $a$-type and odd $b$-type strings is $m-n$. The pair orbit therefore has dimension $m^2+n^2-E=\tfrac12((m+n)^2-E-O)$, half the dimension of the ordinary orbit of $T$. If a string has $r_j$ letters $a$ and $s_j$ letters $b$, then $\min(r_j+s_j,r_k+s_k)=\min(r_j,r_k)+\min(s_j,s_k)$ except for equal odd lengths with opposite endpoint types, where the left side is larger by one. Let $a_l,b_l$ count the odd strings of length $l$ beginning with the two respective letters, and put $\Delta=\sum_{l\text{ odd}}a_lb_l$. The ordinary Jordan centralizer counts now give $\dim O_{(A,B)}=mn+\tfrac12(\dim C_{BA}+\dim C_{AB})-\Delta$. This is a dimension identity for the orbit, not for the full matrix space minus the pair orbit.

**Chain strata.** Stratify $Z$ by its compatible alternating-string diagrams at every link. Compatibility means that the $b$-diagram of one link equals the $a$-diagram of the next. These are finitely many locally closed strata. Pair-orbit projections to either ordinary Jordan orbit are smooth homogeneous fibrations: their fibers are quotients of the ordinary centralizer unit group by the pair stabilizer. Both groups are smooth connected open subsets of finite-dimensional endomorphism spaces, so these fibers are irreducible. Iterating these fibrations proves each nonempty chain stratum $Z_\delta$ smooth and irreducible. The dimension at each fiber-product step is the preceding dimension plus the pair-orbit dimension minus the shared Jordan-orbit dimension. The intermediate orbit dimensions cancel in the formula of step 2.1, giving $\dim Z_\delta=\sum_{i<t}n_in_{i+1}+\tfrac12\dim C_\sigma-\sum_{i<t}\Delta_i$, where $\sigma$ is the type of its final end map.

**Dominance and the top stratum.** The chain equations make $\theta^k$ factor through $U_{t-k}$, so $\operatorname{rank}\theta^k\le n_{t-k}$ and $\theta^t=0$. Thus its type $\sigma$ is dominated by $\eta$ by [F3]. For a $b$-diagram $\sigma$, every row must first be filled internally by alternating $a$ letters; this requires exactly $|\sigma|-\ell(\sigma)$ letters, the size of the diagram obtained by deleting its first column. Over the top diagram $\eta$, this equals $n_{t-1}$, leaving no extra letters: every string starts and ends in $b$ and the lower diagram is exactly the first-column deletion of $\eta$. Repeat down the chain. There is exactly one top stratum; it has both maximal-rank maps at every link, lies in $Z^\circ$, and has every $\Delta_i=0$. Finally, expanding $q_j=n_{t-j+1}-n_{t-j}$ gives $\tfrac12\dim C_\eta=\sum_{i<t}n_in_{i+1}-\sum_{i<t}n_i^2$, so its dimension is $D$.

**Drops of at least four.** By the stratum formula and the nonnegativity of all $\Delta_i$, a final orbit drop of at least four gives $\dim Z_\delta\le\sum n_in_{i+1}+\tfrac12(\dim C_\eta-4)=D-2$. Every non-top stratum has dimension at most $D-1$. This latter estimate establishes uniqueness of the dense top stratum but does not assert that every non-top stratum has codimension two: some are smooth divisors inside $Z^\circ$.

**Drops of two and the nonsmooth-locus bound.** Suppose $\sigma$ is obtained from $\eta$ by moving a box to the next row. Let $\eta'$ and $\sigma'$ denote first-column deletions and let $m=|\eta'|$, $m'=|\sigma'|$. At the last link the available number of $a$ letters is $m$ and its $a$-diagram must be dominated by $\eta'$, since its powers factor through the shorter chain. If the receiving row was nonempty, $m=m'$: internal filling consumes every $a$, all strings begin and end in $b$, and the same next-row degeneration passes to the shorter chain. If a new singleton row is created, $m=m'+1$. After internal filling there is one extra $a$. It can be attached at either end of the shortened last row, at either end of the new singleton $b$ row, or placed in a new singleton $a$ row. No earlier row can receive it: its $a$-diagram would gain a box earlier than the removed last-row box and violate dominance by $\eta'$. In the first four placements one map is maximal rank; the lower diagram is either $\eta'$ or its next-row degeneration. In the fifth placement both maps fail maximal rank, and singleton strings of both types occur, giving $\Delta_i\ge1$. This remains valid when the shortened row is itself a singleton, when there can be more than one singleton $b$. Its homogeneous generators form a regular sequence in the polynomial ring: at the homogeneous maximal ideal, every prefix of length $k$ has height at least $k$, since adjoining the remaining $c-k$ equations raises height by at most $c-k$; the opposite inequality is Krull's bound. Complete the generators to a system of parameters and apply the Cohen-Macaulay parameter theorem in [F4]. Homogeneous localization detects a kernel in a multiplication map, so regularity is global. Each contraction is a product of entries of $AB$, with possible cyclic traces also polynomials in those entries. For rational finite-dimensional $\mathrm{GL}(U)$ modules, the central scalar torus splits the space into integer weight spaces. On each weight space apply the semisimple Lie algebra complete-reducibility theorem [F6] to $\mathfrak{sl}(U)$; an invariant complement then respects the center as well. It respects the group because elementary unipotents and diagonal matrices generate $\mathrm{GL}(U)$. Thus rational quotient invariants lift by complete reducibility in bounded polynomial degree, so the same description applies to a stable closed subscheme with its induced relations. The quotient is consequently the graph over the remaining variables with the induced rank and nilpotency relations, and eliminating the next vertex applies the same one-pair calculation. Repeating leaves precisely the entries of $\theta$. Thus $\mathbb C[Z]^H$ is generated by those entries, and is the coordinate ring of the closure of $\theta(Z)$. **Normality and boundary of the orbit closure.** An element of $\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb C[Z]^H)$ integral over $\mathbb C[Z]^H$ is also integral over the normal domain $\mathbb C[Z]$, hence belongs to it. Being a fraction of invariant elements it is fixed by $H$, so it belongs to $\mathbb C[Z]^H$; no equality between the full invariant fraction field and the fraction field of the invariant ring is needed. Therefore $\mathbb C[X]$ is a normal domain, reduced and irreducible. The finitely many boundary nilpotent orbits have positive even dimension drops by step 1.4, so their union has codimension at least two. The point cases and their empty boundary were proved in step 1.1. This proves all chain and orbit conclusions.

$\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ of its conjugacy orbit
([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]]), and let
$\partial X=X\setminus\mathrm{GL}(V)\cdot e$. Then $\mathbb C[X]$ is a reduced
irreducible normal domain and $\operatorname{codim}_X\partial X\ge2$. This
holds for every Jordan type, not only the regular nilpotent cone.

lengths $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_t>0$, put $n_i=q_t+\cdots+q_{t-i+1}$ and

with coordinates $(A_i,B_i)$ and let $Z\subseteq M$ be the closed subscheme
$B_1A_1=0$, $B_iA_i=A_{i-1}B_{i-1}$ $(2\le i<t)$. Then $Z$ is a complete
intersection, smooth outside a closed subset of codimension $\ge2$, reduced,
irreducible and normal, and the invariant ring $\mathbb C[Z]^H$ under
$H=\prod_{i<t}\mathrm{GL}(U_i)$ is the coordinate ring of $X$ via the end map
$\theta=A_{t-1}B_{t-1}$.

The unique endomorphism of the zero space is nilpotent. With the same least-positive-exponent convention, its nilpotency index is $1$ because its identity and zero endomorphisms coincide.

$R$-module. Then
$$\operatorname{depth}(M)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathfrak m\in\operatorname{Ass}_R(M).$$

$R$-module, and let $S \subseteq R$ be multiplicative. Then
$$ \operatorname{Ass}_{S^{-1}R}(S^{-1}M)=\{S^{-1}\mathfrak p : \mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Ass}_R(M),\ \mathfrak p \cap S=\varnothing\}. $$

$$\operatorname{depth}_I(M/xM)=\operatorname{depth}_I(M)-1,$$
with $\infty-1=\infty$.

$$ \bigcup_{\mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Ass}_R(M)}\mathfrak p. $$
If the Axiom of Choice also holds and $M$ is finitely generated, this is a finite union.

$$ I\subseteq \mathfrak p_1\cup\cdots\cup \mathfrak p_n, $$
then $I\subseteq \mathfrak p_i$ for some $i$.

Lie algebra over any characteristic-zero field is completely reducible.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space, let $n\ge0$, and let
$E:=V^{\otimes n}$ carry the left place action of $S_n$
([[def-commuting-symmetric-and-linear-actions-on-tensor-power]]). Let $A$ be
the image of the algebra homomorphism $\mathbb C[S_n]\to\operatorname{End}(E)$
extending the place action, and let
$B:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{g^{\otimes n}:g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)\}$
be the linear span of the diagonal operators
$g^{\otimes n}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=gv_1\otimes\cdots\otimes gv_n$.
Then:

1. **(Mutual centralizers.)** $B=\{F\in\operatorname{End}(E):F a=aF\text{ for
   all }a\in A\}$ and $A=\{F\in\operatorname{End}(E):F b=bF\text{ for all
   }b\in B\}$.

   $\mathbb C$-subalgebra of $\operatorname{End}(E)$ and equals the image of
   the diagonal action of the universal enveloping algebra
   $U(\mathfrak{gl}(V))$, that is the unital subalgebra generated by the
   operators $\Delta(T)=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes T\otimes

   ([[lem-tensor-place-operators-span-the-symmetric-centralizer]]).

All statements include $n=0$, where $E=\mathbb C$.

All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are
Lie subalgebras of $\mathfrak{gl}_m(\mathbb C)=M_m(\mathbb C)$ in the sense of
[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in
each case by the computation displayed.

* The **general linear Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)=M_n(\mathbb C)$,
  for $n\ge1$. The **special linear Lie algebra**
  $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$
  is a Lie subalgebra because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$, and
  $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ agrees with
  [[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]].
* The **symplectic Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ is the set of
  $A\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ with $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$.
* The **orthogonal Lie algebras** $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
  $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ are the sets of $A\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ with
  $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for
  $m=2n$ and
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&I_n\\0&I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $m=2n+1$.

Solving $AJ+JA^{T}=0$ blockwise gives
$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ for the symplectic and even
orthogonal cases, with $b,c$ symmetric for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
$b,c$ skew-symmetric for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$, and gives
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&u&-w^{T}\\ w&a&b\\ -u^{T}&c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix},\qquad u\in M_{1\times n}(\mathbb C),\quad w\in M_{n\times1}(\mathbb C),\quad b,c\ \text{skew-symmetric},$$
for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$. In particular
$\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n+1)=\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$
and $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n-1)$. Each set is closed under the
bracket: if $AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$, then
$[A,B]J+J[A,B]^{T}=ABJ-BAJ+JB^{T}A^{T}-JA^{T}B^{T}$, and substituting

$M_m(\mathbb C)$ closed under the commutator, hence a Lie subalgebra.

$$\bigl(e_i\otimes f_j\bigr)_{(i,j)\in I\times J}.$$
